title: Editing and Omission
subject: english_grammar
syllabus_note: Integrated board practice for the CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184) Section B Grammar: identifying and correcting errors and missing words across tenses, modals, concord, determiners and reported speech.

blocks.title: Can you spot it in ten seconds?
blocks.body:
*My brother and me goes to the same school since 2020.*

This short sentence has **two** errors: the subject pronoun must be *I* (*My brother and **I***), and *since 2020* with two subjects needs *have been going* instead of *goes*. In the board exam you get one line at a time, and you must find the error and write the correction quickly and neatly.

Editing and omission bring together everything you have learnt: tenses, modals, concord, determiners, reported speech, plus prepositions and word forms. This chapter gives you a step-by-step detective method and a large set of board-style lines to practise until spotting errors becomes automatic.

blocks.title: The editor who loved clear English
blocks.body:
Khushwant Singh edited *The Illustrated Weekly of India* and later the *Hindustan Times*, and wrote the novel *Train to Pakistan*. As an editor, his job every day was to read other people's writing and fix errors before millions of readers saw them.

He wrote his famous column *With Malice towards One and All* for decades, and received the Padma Vibhushan in 2007. Every good editor starts as a careful detective of small mistakes.
blocks.future: Editing skills lead to careers in publishing, journalism, content strategy, law (drafting) and translation, and help in every exam you write.

blocks.question: Which word is wrong? *She is good in drawing.*
blocks.explanation: We are *good at* a skill: *She is good at drawing.* Preposition errors are a favourite in board editing.

blocks.title: How to edit a line
blocks.body:
**Board format:** each sentence or line has **one** error. You must write the **incorrect word** and the **correction**, usually in a table or as *incorrect → correct*.

**Method:**
1. Read the whole line (and the line before it, if it is a passage) for meaning.
2. **Find the subject and the verb first.** Most errors are in the verb: tense, agreement, or form after a helper.
3. Then check, in order: **articles/determiners → prepositions → pronouns → conjunctions → word forms → plurals → comparatives**.
4. Change **only one word** (or the smallest group) and keep the meaning.
5. Read the corrected line again; it must now be perfect.

**Spelling and punctuation:** copy your correction exactly; a misspelt correction loses the mark.

blocks.title: The 10-point error checklist
blocks.body:
| Step | Look at | Typical error | Correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Verb tense** | *Yesterday he **goes** home.* | goes → went |
| 2 | **Subject-verb agreement** | *The list of names **are** long.* | are → is |
| 3 | **Verb form after a helper** | *She **can sings**; he **did not came**.* | sings → sing; came → come |
| 4 | **Articles / determiners** | *He is **a** honest man; **less** students.* | a → an; less → fewer |
| 5 | **Prepositions** | *He is good **in** maths; married **with** her.* | in → at; with → to |
| 6 | **Pronouns** | *Between you and **I**; everyone did **their** best* (formal) | I → me |
| 7 | **Conjunctions** | *Although he was ill, **but** he came.* | remove *but* / but → (none) |
| 8 | **Word form** | *She sings **beautiful**.* | beautiful → beautifully |
| 9 | **Singular / plural** | *one of my **friend**; two **childs*** | friend → friends; childs → children |
| 10 | **Comparatives** | ***more better**; the **most tallest*** | more better → better |

blocks.question: Edit the line: *The children was playing in the garden.*
option_feedback: *were playing* is fine; the problem is agreement.
Changing the subject changes the meaning; correct the verb.

blocks.title: Fixed prepositions examiners test
blocks.body:
| Phrase | Correct preposition |
|---|---|
| good / bad / expert ___ (a skill) | **at**: *good at maths* |
| interested ___ | **in** |
| afraid / proud / fond / tired ___ | **of** |
| married / similar / addicted / prefer A ___ B | **to** |
| different ___ | **from** |
| angry ___ a person / ___ a thing | **with** a person / **at** or **about** a thing |
| depend / rely ___ | **on** |
| congratulate ___ | **on** |
| responsible ___ | **for** |
| born ___ (year/month) / ___ (date) | **in** 2010 / **on** 5 May |
| arrive ___ (city) / ___ (place) | **in** Delhi / **at** the station |
| discuss / enter / reach / attend ___ | **no preposition**: *discuss the plan*, *reach home* |

blocks.title: Word forms: noun, verb, adjective, adverb
blocks.body:
Many editing errors use the right word in the wrong form:

- **Adjective vs adverb:** an adjective describes a noun (*a **careful** driver*); an adverb describes a verb (*He drives **carefully***). ✗ *She speaks fluent.* ✓ *She speaks fluently.*
- **Noun vs verb:** *advice* (noun) / *advise* (verb); *practice* (noun) / *practise* (verb); *success* (noun) / *succeed* (verb) / *successful* (adjective).
  ✗ *He gave me good advise.* ✓ *He gave me good advice.*
- **Comparatives:** never double them. ✗ *more taller, most best* ✓ *taller, best*. Use *than* after a comparative: ✗ *superior than* ✓ *superior **to***.
- **Irregular plurals:** *child → children, man → men, mouse → mice, criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena*.
- **Pronoun case:** after a preposition use the object form: *between you and **me***, *for **him** and **me***.

blocks.question: Edit the line: *She danced so graceful that everyone clapped.*
Edit the line: *My grandfather is fond in gardening.*
option_feedback: The present is fine for a hobby he still has.

blocks.title: Where words go missing
blocks.body:
In an **omission** task, one word has been left out of each line. You must say **which word is missing and where**, usually by writing the word before, the missing word, and the word after.

**Method:**
1. Read the line aloud in your head; you will feel a "bump" where the word is missing.
2. Check the grammar skeleton: every finite verb needs its helper (*is/are/have/has/will*); every singular countable noun needs a determiner; every verb + infinitive needs *to*.
3. The missing word is usually small: an **article, preposition, helping verb, pronoun, conjunction or *to***.

blocks.title: The usual missing words
blocks.body:
| Word that often goes missing | Example with the gap (^) | Correct |
|---|---|---|
| article | *She is ^ best player.* | the |
| helping verb | *They ^ playing in the park.* | are |
| preposition | *He was born ^ 2010.* | in |
| *to* (infinitive) | *I want ^ learn music.* | to |
| pronoun | *Ravi told ^ that he was busy.* | me |
| conjunction | *She was tired ^ she kept working.* | but |
| *of / for / with* after nouns | *a cup ^ tea* | of |
| *have / has* in perfect tenses | *I ^ finished my work.* | have |

blocks.question: Which word is missing? *We have been waiting the bus for an hour.*
blocks.explanation: *wait for* someone or something: *waiting for the bus*.
option_feedback: *have been waiting* is a complete verb.

blocks.title: Editing a passage line by line
blocks.problem:
The following passage has one error in each line. Write the incorrect word and the correction.

1. Exercise is very important for a healthy life. It keep
2. our body fit and our mind fresh. Doctors advices that
3. we should walk atleast thirty minutes every day. Many
4. people does not exercise because they think they have no time.
steps: Line 2: *Doctors* is plural, and *advice* is a noun; the verb is *advise* → **advices → advise**.
Line 3: *at least* is two words → **atleast → at least**.
blocks.answer: keep → keeps; advices → advise; atleast → at least; does → do

blocks.title: Omission line by line
blocks.problem:
One word is missing in each line. Write the word before, the missing word and the word after.

1. Rani is one of best dancers in our school.
2. She has been learning Kathak the age of six.
3. Last year she won first prize at a national festival.
4. She wants become a dance teacher.
steps: 2. A point of time with the perfect continuous → *since*: *Kathak **since** the*.
blocks.answer: of the best; Kathak since the; won the first; wants to become

blocks.question: Edit the line: *Neither of the answers are correct, so try again.*
option_feedback: *Neither of the* needs a plural noun.

blocks.title: The VAPPCW scan
blocks.body:
Scan every line in this order:

- **V**erb (tense, agreement, form after helper)
- **A**rticle / determiner
- **P**reposition
- **P**ronoun
- **C**onjunction (double conjunctions: *although … but*, *though … yet* is fine)
- **W**ord form (adjective/adverb, noun/verb, plurals, comparatives)

"**V**ery **A**ngry **P**eople **P**ick **C**orrect **W**ords."

blocks.title: Mistakes students make in editing answers
blocks.body:
1. Changing two words when only one is wrong.
2. Writing the correction with a new error (wrong spelling).
3. Changing the meaning of the sentence instead of correcting the grammar.
4. Not copying the incorrect word exactly as it appears.
5. In omission, writing only the missing word and not showing where it goes (write the words before and after).
6. Ignoring the line before: in a passage, the tense is often set by the earlier line.
7. Leaving a blank: always write your best guess; there is no negative marking.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Run an **"Error auction"**: put ten sentences on the board, some correct and some with one error. Teams get 100 points to "bid" on sentences they think are correct. Then reveal the answers; teams win points for correct bids and lose them for wrong ones. Students quickly learn to check verbs, articles and prepositions before betting.

blocks.title: Say it in your own words
blocks.body: Which grammar area gives you the most errors in your own writing: verbs, articles or prepositions? Write two sentences you often get wrong, and correct them.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapters 1–4 and Determiners:** every rule you learnt there is tested here.
- **Chapter 7, Gap Filling:** the same rules, but you supply the word instead of correcting it.
- **Your own writing:** use the VAPPCW scan to proofread your letters and paragraphs before the exam ends.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
Edit each line (one error per line):

(a) The news are not good today.
(b) She is more cleverer than her sister.
(c) He has gone to Mumbai last week.
(d) Each of the boys have a bicycle.
(e) I am looking forward to meet you.

**Answer:** (a) **are → is** (b) **more cleverer → cleverer** (c) **has gone → went** (d) **have → has** (e) **meet → meeting** (*look forward to* + V-ing).

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Each board line has one error (editing) or one missing word (omission).
- Check the verb first, then determiners, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions and word forms.
- Write the incorrect word and the correction exactly; for omission, show where the word goes.
- Missing words are usually articles, prepositions, helping verbs, *to*, pronouns or conjunctions.
- Learn the fixed prepositions (*good at, fond of, married to, different from, depend on*).

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Spend about one minute per line; come back to difficult lines later.
- If a line looks correct, check prepositions and articles again; there is always one error.
- Answer in the format asked: usually *incorrect word → correct word*.
- Never rewrite the whole sentence unless asked.

blocks.front: Correct: *Although it rained, but we played.*
Correct: *I look forward to see you.*
What usually goes missing in omission?
blocks.back: Articles, prepositions, helping verbs, *to*, pronouns, conjunctions.
